In my dream I was seeing in that night [and behold, a garden ...] gardeners, and they were watering [... a hundred trees, and there went out] great roots from their bases [...] all the water, and a fire was burning in the whole [garden ...].

Symbolic meaning (within the Book of Giants/Enochic context):
- The garden: a cosmic/paradisal garden (often aligned with Eden or the divine planting), a symbol of the ordered world under divine care and the sphere of life bestowed by God.
- The trees (maten ʾilanin; “a hundred trees”): figures for the “great ones”—the Watchers and/or their giant offspring—emphasizing stature and rooted establishment (“great roots from their bases”). In related Enochic traditions, trees regularly symbolize rulers or mighty beings.
- The water: first as irrigation under the “gardeners” (agents of divine oversight), but in the dream sequence it also portends the deluge—overwhelming waters as judgment that will undo the giants’ established “roots.”
- The fire: paired with the water as a second mode of judgment—consuming fire that devastates the garden. In Enochic literature, fiery judgment accompanies or follows the flood to signify comprehensive, divinely sent destruction of the rebellious beings.

Together, the imagery signals that the ordered realm (the garden) containing the mighty ones (trees) will be subjected to total divine judgment by both water (flood) and fire (conflagration), leaving no security even for those with “great roots.” The “gardeners” function as agents of divine administration, underscoring that what appears nurtured and secure is nonetheless destined for judgment.
